activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: The law of demand says that when the price of something rises, people buy less of it, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
The price sign at Marigold Farm's stand had said four dollars a basket all June, and the line had stretched past the honey table every Saturday. Now, in the last week of July, the sign said eight dollars, and Emilie stood behind the baskets with nothing to do but rearrange them. Ms. Chan, who owned the stand, had told her that morning that a late frost had ruined half the crop. "Fewer berries means a higher price," she had said, and then walked off to the truck, leaving Emilie to work the counter alone.

By eleven, Emilie had sold four baskets in an hour. The week before, she had sold forty in the same time. She watched a woman pick up a basket, look at the sign, set it back down, and drift toward the apple cider stand as though nothing had happened. Then Brennan appeared at the front of what used to be the line, holding his bike helmet under one arm.

"Why is nobody buying?" he asked. "You're famous. People used to fight over these."

"Eight dollars," Emilie said. "It was four."

Brennan frowned at the sign like it had insulted him personally. "So people just... stopped?"

"Not stopped. Slowed down." Emilie pulled her notebook out from under the cash box, where she had been keeping a tally. She liked to classify her customers in columns: big buyers, browsers, regulars. The regulars were still coming. It was the browsers who had vanished. She flipped back to her page from last Saturday, counted the tallies twice, and then looked up, because a shape was forming in her head that she hadn't put there herself. "When the price went up, people bought less. Exactly less. Not one other thing about the berries changed. Same baskets, same taste, same me behind the table."

"So charge four dollars again," Brennan said, with the confidence of someone who had never inventoried anything.

"I can't. There aren't enough berries." Emilie glanced toward the truck, where Ms. Chan was stacking empty crates. Her instinct was to go ask her boss to lower the price anyway, but she had done something like that once before, at her school bake sale, and had watched half the table get cleared out in twenty minutes with nothing left for the people who came late. She'd felt bad about that for weeks, though even now she wasn't sure the smaller portions had been the right fix either.

A man in a gardening hat walked up, read the sign, and bought one basket instead of the four he'd bought last weekend, according to her notes. "Still worth it," he told her, "but one's all I need at this price."

"See?" Emilie whispered to Brennan. "The law of demand. Price goes up, people buy less, as long as nothing else changes."

Brennan leaned over the baskets, took out his wallet, and counted out eight dollars. "One basket," he said. "Proving you right costs me my whole allowance."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Puberty is driven by hormones: the pituitary gland in the brain signals the ovaries or testes to make more estrogen or testosterone.
story:
Emily stood at the bathroom sink after gym class, staring at the deodorant stick in her hand like it might go off. Last week Rita had leaned over in science and whispered, "You might want some of this," and Emily had wanted to sink through the floor. She had thought about it for three days before buying one at the drugstore, and now she didn't even know if she was using it right.

She twisted the dial and sniffed it, then sniffed her own shoulder. Definitely needed. She swiped it on, twice on each side, and caught Arwa's eye in the mirror. Arwa was retying her ponytail at the next sink.

"You don't have to do it like it's poison," Arwa said. "Just regular."

"It's weird," Emily said. "Last year I never smelled like anything. Why now?"

Arwa shrugged. "My cousin asked the doctor that once. She said it's hormones. The pituitary gland, that's in your brain, signals the ovaries or the testes to make more estrogen or testosterone. That's what tells the body it's time for puberty. It's like a starter pistol nobody can hear."

"A component of the brain just decides," Emily said slowly, watching her own face in the mirror. Something invisible, in there behind her eyebrows, sending orders to parts of her she couldn't see either. She thought of her mom's voice last month: "You're growing, that's all." Growing, like it was one nutritious meal doing all the work. It wasn't. It was a message, a chain of messages, already underway whether she anticipated them or not.

"So the sweat glands get the message too," she said. She rolled the stick under her arm once more, testing whether twice a day would be enough, whether she'd have to redo it after practice. "Invisible cause, visible smell."

"Basically," Arwa said, snapping her ponytail holder. "Also, your armpits. Not your shoulder."

Emily laughed, rubbed it in with her sleeve, and dropped the stick in her backpack's front pocket where she'd find it at lunch.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Puberty usually begins between ages 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys, and starting anywhere in that range is normal.
story:
The smell problem started on Tuesday, when Jayda slid her chair two inches away from Nicolas during science and said, "No offense, but did you run here?"

He had not run. After school he conducted an experiment, because experiments were his principle for solving things: change one thing, watch what happens. On Wednesday he showered and wore deodorant. Jayda slid her chair closer. On Thursday he skipped both. Moshe opened a window and fanned himself with a worksheet. On Friday he showered but skipped the deodorant, and Jayda compromised by sitting sideways.

"It's the sweat glands," Moshe said at lunch, chewing his sandwich with the calm of someone stating the weather. "Puberty turns them up. My brother went through it. We called his room the Swamp."

"I haven't even started puberty," Nicolas said. "I'm the shortest kid in class. Every single one of you is taller. Jayda got taller in September. Moshe got taller twice."

Moshe shrugged. "You could ask a doctor. My mom asked about my brother, because she thought something was wrong with him. The doctor said puberty usually starts between ages 8 and 13 in girls and between ages 9 and 14 in boys, and starting anywhere in that range is normal. So my brother was just on the late end. Then he shot up a foot."

Nicolas did the math on his napkin. Nine was the bottom of the boys' range and fourteen was the top, which meant the whole thing ran late for boys anyway, and eleven, where he was, sat right in the middle of it. So his sweat glands could be switching on before anything else even showed. The smell had arrived early, like a delivery truck before the furniture.

He kept his objective simple: nobody moves their chair on Monday. He set a phone alarm for 6:40, showered every morning, and put the deodorant on top of his toothbrush so he couldn't miss it. He even wrote a sign on the bathroom mirror that said SWAMP, which his dad found confusing but decided not to enforce any rules about.

Monday, in science, he sat down and waited. Jayda didn't move. Neither did Moshe, who leaned over and sniffed the air like a bloodhound.

"Cool waterfall scent," Moshe said.

"It's called Alpine Rush, thank you."

Ms. Wanjiru walked past their table, paused, and said, "Somebody in this room smells better than usual." Nicolas raised his hand.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Each degree of latitude or longitude is divided into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds, to pinpoint an exact spot.
story:
Bentley sat in the back seat with the atlas open across his knees, tracing the thin curved lines with one finger. Their whole trip depended on this map, because his phone had died somewhere outside Amarillo and his dad refused to stop and ask for directions. "We're meeting Mr. Popescu at the fossil site near the city," his dad had said that morning, "so figure out where that is, because I'll be driving." Next to Bentley, his friend Mckenna leaned over the map, though what she really wanted was to find the biggest city they would pass through so she could add it to the list of places she'd been, a list she was building in a notebook she guarded like treasure.

The fossil site instructions included a coordinate: 35 degrees, 12 minutes north, 103 degrees, 40 minutes west. Bentley squinted at it. "Minutes? Why minutes? Is Mr. Popescu going to move the fossils in fifteen minutes or something?" Mckenna laughed and said the verdict on his theory was no, because seconds were there too, and you couldn't be late by a few seconds to a patch of ground. Bentley felt a sting of envy that she had spotted that first. He looked at the numbers again and began to wonder if minutes might not be time at all.

He tested the idea the only way he could. He found 35 degrees north on the side of the map and slid his finger across, then found 103 degrees west along the top and slid down until the lines crossed. That single point covered a huge area, half of New Mexico, way too big to be a fossil site. "So one degree isn't small enough," he said slowly. "They had to cut it up." He counted the tiny tick marks between the numbered lines and found sixty of them. Mckenna counted the even tinier marks between one tick and the next and got sixty again. "It's like a clock," she said. "Each degree is divided into sixty minutes, and each minute into sixty seconds."

"To pinpoint an exact spot," Bentley said. He ran his finger 12 of the small ticks past 35 degrees and 40 ticks past 103 degrees west, and the point landed on a little brown patch near the city with a tiny fossil symbol beside it. He checked the name against the instructions and they matched. He wrote the coordinate on a scrap of paper and passed it up to the front seat so his dad could put it in the GPS once the phone charged. The scrap looked small and anonymous, just numbers, but it was the whole site in a handful of symbols.

Mckenna found the biggest city on their route and copied it into her notebook with a flourish, then held the page up for Bentley to see. "Add the coordinate," he said. "Nobody else will know what the numbers mean." She wrote 35 degrees, 12 minutes north underneath the city's name, and Bentley leaned over to check that her sixes were facing the right way. "Sixty seconds in one minute," she said, tapping the last line. "Got it memorized."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: In "divide and choose," one person splits something into two parts and the other picks first, so the divider has a reason to make the parts equal.
story:
Adam slid into his chair at the dinner table so fast he nearly knocked over his glass of milk. "Dad, I need help, and I need it before Saturday."

"What's Saturday?" his dad asked, spooning rice onto Adam's plate.

"The rematch. Me and Pearl and Talya, basketball at the park. Last week we argued the whole time about who got the good ball, the one with the grip. Pearl grabbed it first, Talya said that was arbitrary, and then we wasted half an hour fighting instead of playing." Adam tore a piece of flatbread in half. "Mr. Aziz says if we keep this up, nobody will even want to come."

His little brother, mouth full, said, "Just take turns."

"That's what we tried. But then we argued about who goes first." Adam pushed his peas around his plate, thinking so hard he forgot to eat. "There has to be a rule that works for everybody."

His mom set down a plate of baklava, still warm, the honey shining under the kitchen light. There were two pieces left, and his brother reached for the bigger one at the exact moment Adam did.

"Hey!" they both said.

Their mom held up the plate. "One of you split them, then the other picks first."

Adam froze, fork in the air. "Wait. Say that again."

"Split, then the other picks. That's how my mother did it."

Adam stared at the baklava, and it hit him like a buzzer beater. If he cut the pieces and his brother chose, Adam would cut them exactly equal, because any uneven piece would vanish down his brother's throat first. It worked both ways. Whoever cut had to be fair, or lose out. "That's it!" He jumped up so fast his chair scraped the floor. He grabbed a napkin and scribbled: "Pearl. New plan for Saturday. One of us splits, other picks first. Try it with the ball rotation, everything. Bring Talya. Adam." He ran it to the mailbox before dinner got cold.

Saturday morning, he found Pearl and Talya already at the park, ball in Talya's hands. "We got your note," Pearl said. "So here's what we did. I split the warm-up time into two chunks, and Talya picked first. Then we traded. Talya picked who holds the good ball first half, I picked second."

"And it actually worked," Talya said, spinning the ball on one finger. "No yelling. Mr. Aziz stopped by and watched for ten minutes. He said our Saturday games might outlast the Lakers."

"He said we could be a dynasty," Pearl said. "His word."

"Then let's earn it," Adam said, and stole the ball clean out of the air.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Preheating means waiting until the oven has reached the set temperature before the batter goes in, so baking starts at the right heat.
story:
Alex slid the muffin tray into the oven and set the dial to 375, feeling proud of how fast he'd moved. "Done in five minutes," he announced. "Batter, tray, oven. Nobody can say I'm slow."

Crystal looked up from her notebook, where she'd written every step of Ms. Suryanto's recipe in careful blue ink. "Alex, I don't think that's how it works. Ms. Suryanto said something about the oven before we started."

"She said set it to 375," Alex said. "It's set."

Yaseen peered through the oven door. "There's no glow yet. No heat coming off it either." He waved his hand near the vent, then pulled it back and blew on his fingers. "Okay, there's a little. Barely."

Alex folded his arms. The two of them had a habit of doubting him, and he was getting tired of it. Yaseen's skepticism had ruined his last three ideas, and Alex had half a mind to boycott the whole baking lesson if this kept up. "It's warming up right now," he said. "Every second counts."

Twenty-five minutes later, Ms. Suryanto came around the counter with her timer in hand. She opened the oven, and all three of them stared at the tray. The muffins had risen crookedly, one of them lumpy and pale on one side, the tops flat and dense where they should have domed.

"Interesting," Ms. Suryanto said, though her face suggested something other than interest. She touched the side of the oven with the back of her hand. "You put these in before the little light went off, didn't you."

"The little light?" Alex said.

She pointed to a small orange bulb above the dial, steady and unblinking. "Preheating means waiting until the oven has reached the set temperature before the batter goes in, so baking starts at the right heat." She said it lightly, the way someone mentions rain, and moved on to check Crystal's tray.

Alex stood there turning it over in his mind. The oven hadn't been at 375 when his batter went in. It had been climbing toward it, and his muffins had baked in a rising heat instead of the right heat. He looked at the orange bulb, then at his sad crooked muffins, and a small test formed in his head. If the light was the problem, then waiting for the light should fix it. Simple as that.

He mixed a new batch of batter, more carefully this time, and set the dial again. When the orange bulb still glowed, he sat on the counter stool and waited, drumming his fingers, watching it like a hawk watches a field. Crystal set her finished muffins on the rack to cool, their tops a distinct golden brown, and Yaseen quietly slid the mixing bowl closer so Alex could reach the spoon without standing up.

The bulb blinked off. Alex checked it twice, then slid his tray in and shut the door.

Twenty-three minutes later he pulled out twelve muffins, evenly domed, and set one, still warm, on a napkin beside Crystal's elbow without a word.

She broke it in half and looked at the soft, even crumb inside. "Okay," she said. "You get the first one of the next batch."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: In the rock cycle, any type of rock can become any other type, through melting, weathering, or heat and pressure.
story:
Landon pressed his nose against the display case in the science museum's rock hall, where a sign announced the Junior Geologist Challenge: sort twelve mystery rocks in twenty minutes, and the winner's class would get a scholarship for a field trip to the quarry. The clock above the table had already started. "Any rock can become any other kind," he whispered to Tiago. "That's the problem. They're all mixed up because of it."

"Mixed up how?" Tiago asked, turning a gray stone over in his hand.

"Because nothing stays one thing forever." Landon picked up a chunk with sparkles pressed into bands. "Igneous comes from melting, sedimentary builds up from bits, and metamorphic gets squeezed by heat and pressure. But any of them can turn into any other one. This banded stuff used to be something else before the squeezing." He held it against the card marked metamorphic. Tiago nodded and slid a gritty, layered rock toward sedimentary, since it looked glued together from grains.

Their classmate Nikolas, who had been scrambling at the far end of the table, hurried over with a smooth black stone. "I put this under igneous, but I think I violate the rules if I change my answers now," he said. The museum guide, Mr. Wright, shook his head. "Changes are allowed until the buzzer. That's how the rock cycle works too, you know." Nikolas laughed and moved his rock, and Landon checked each sample once more, thinking about which path it might have traveled: melted, weathered, or squeezed.

The buzzer sounded. Mr. Wright walked the table slowly, then held up Landon's banded chunk. "Correct. And this one fooled people all day." He announced that all three boys had earned the scholarship, and the class cheered from behind the rope. On the wall behind the table hung a photo of an influential geologist who had studied this very cycle, and Tiago pointed at it and grinned. "Next year, that's you up there." Landon slid the banded rock into his pocket, with Mr. Wright's blessing, and held it up to the light.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Scoring a line on thick card with a blunt tool before folding it gives a straight, clean fold instead of a cracked, bumpy one.
story:
Emilia sat at the kitchen table with three ruined cards in front of her. Each one was a folded half-sheet of thick card, and each fold had cracked along the crease, pale fibres showing through the blue like a scratch. She had pressed hard with her thumb, then with the edge of a ruler, and the folds still came out bumpy and split. Tomorrow was Aleah's birthday, and Emilia wanted to give her a card that looked like the ones in the shop window, smooth and clean.

She picked up the worst card and turned it toward the window light. The crack ran along the fold, but only along the fold. The rest of the card was perfect. So the card was not too weak all over; something about the fold itself was going wrong. She thought about the shop cards. She had never seen one cracked, and their folds were sharp, almost like a thin line had been drawn down them first. Maybe the paper had not been folded cold. Maybe something had been done to the card before the fold, something she could not see, like a hidden step.

She tried an experiment. On a fresh piece of the same thick card, she took the blunt end of a spoon and, with a ruler as a guide, drew the spoon firmly down the card once, pressing a shallow line where the fold would go. Then she folded along that line. The card turned over sharp and neat, the crease smooth and blue on both sides, no crack, no bump. Emilia ran her finger along it. It felt like the edge of an envelope.

Just then her little brother barged in, grabbed a spoon, and started mashing his cereal at the table. He was not being wicked, only negligent, as usual, milk slopping toward her cards. Emilia rescued them and carried her project to her room, where she made the real card, a rocket in silver pen with "Happy Birthday Aleah" inside. She scored the fold first, then folded, and watched the plain card transform into something that looked bought, not made.

At school the next morning, Zariah leaned over Emilia's desk and frowned at the card. "How'd you get the fold like that?" Emilia held it up. "You score it," she said, "with something blunt, before you fold." Zariah tilted her head. "Show me at lunch?" Emilia slid the card into Aleah's hands and grinned. "Bring a spoon."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: During a side breath in front crawl, skilled swimmers keep one goggle lens in the water and turn only far enough for the mouth to clear the surface.
story:
Muhammad lay on the scratchy outfield grass of the baseball diamond, arms windmilling in slow motion, cheek pressed to the ground. "You look like a bug," said Aniya, sitting cross-legged beside him with her stopwatch. "A bug that's about to swim twenty-five metres. Saturday's the test, so be nice." Saturday felt close. Two weeks ago, in the shallow end, he had turned his whole face up to the sky at every breath, and by the flags he was gasping, arms dead, the coach's whistle ringing in his ears. He had failed that day, and he did not want to feel that way again in front of the whole class.

Brendan jogged over from first base, where he had been practicing throws against the backstop. He was the fastest swimmer in grade five, and Muhammad had watched him all season. "You're turning too far," Brendan said, dropping onto the grass. "Watch what my face does." He mimed a stroke, and his head rotated just a sliver, like a door opening a crack. "One goggle lens stays in the water, and you turn only far enough for your mouth to clear the surface. That's it." Muhammad copied the motion, cheek grazing the grass, one eye down, mouth tilted to where the sky would be.

He thought about it while he drilled. When his face went all the way up, the rest of him sank and dragged, like the day at the flags. When he rotated just that crack, everything stayed long and smooth, the way he had seen it without understanding it. He tested the idea on dry land, ten strokes, twenty, mouth opening to a practiced half turn. Aniya called encouragement between counts, and even a spontaneous cheer from a passing parent on the way to the bleachers made him grin without stopping.

By the time the sun went orange behind the scoreboard, Muhammad could do the whole pattern without thinking. The hierarchy of his worries had rearranged itself: breathing, once at the top, had dropped below nerves, maybe below nothing at all. Saturday, the water would be cool and clear, and somewhere past the flags his hand would touch the wall. "Fifty-eight seconds on grass," Aniya announced, clicking the stopwatch. "Now go again."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures, so a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent.
story:
Colton had one job at the town hall meeting: narrate the class presentation on how a bill becomes a law, and he had practiced until his little sister could recite it. The room smelled like wet umbrellas, because outside a monsoon of rain was hammering the roof, and half the audience had arrived dripping. Mr. Halvorsen had booked the hall so the students could present to the actual town council, which made Colton's stomach feel like it was full of moths.

He got through the federal part fine. "First the House of Commons passes the bill," he said, "then the Senate passes it, then it gets royal assent and becomes law." Then Quinn held up their second poster, the one about provincial bills, and Colton stopped. The poster showed only one chamber, one box, with an arrow to royal assent. He stared at it, certain they had left a step out. Federal bills went through two houses. Provincial ones should too, shouldn't they?

He looked at Mr. Halvorsen, who only raised an eyebrow and gave him a small nod, the kind that meant keep going. So Colton did the only thing he could think of: he tested it out loud. "We checked this twice," he said, "because it looked wrong to us too. In every Canadian province, the legislature has just one chamber. So a provincial bill passes only that one house, and then the lieutenant governor gives royal assent. Fewer steps than a federal bill."

From the front row, Elisha shot her hand up. "That's why the provincial poster is thinner!" she said, waving the frugal little booklet they'd printed, all four pages of it. "I thought we ran out of ink." A council member laughed and called it "the cheapest civics lesson in town," and Colton felt the moths in his stomach settle down and go to sleep.

After the meeting, an old man in a rain jacket stopped by the poster table. He said he'd been watching council meetings for forty years and had never once heard a kid explain the provincial part that clearly. Colton rolled up the thin poster, careful with the corners, and handed it over.

"Keep it," the man said. "I'll hang it up where the rain can't get it."

activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
knowledge_domain: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
fact: In F. Scott Fitzgerald's novel The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, a green light glows at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock, across the water from Gatsby's house.
story:
Noemie had promised her book club that by Thursday she would bring one chart, and Thursday was tomorrow. The chart was supposed to show how a single symbol in The Great Gatsby changed meaning from chapter to chapter, and so far her poster board held one sad green line and the word "hope?" with a question mark she now regretted.

She had invited Noel and Kaitlin over after school because misery was cheaper in bulk. They sat on her living room rug with the novel open between them, three bags of chips, and a deadline.

"Chapter one," said Noel, flipping pages. "On the very first night of the story, Gatsby is reaching toward something out on the water. A green light."

Noemie leaned over. "Where exactly? The book has to say."

Kaitlin found it and read aloud. The light glowed at the end of a dock, and the dock belonged to Daisy Buchanan, whose house sat across the water from Gatsby's. "So he's standing in his yard," Kaitlin said slowly, "reaching for a light on her dock."

"That's just a weird thing a neighbor does," said Noel.

"No," said Noemie. She got her marker and wrote it down, because writing it down made it feel more like a discovery and less like a guess. "It's not just a light. In chapter one it's far away and he can't have it. Watch what happens to it later."

They hunted through the book, passing chapters back and forth like a card game. The green light kept turning up, but each time it seemed to mean something slightly different, and Noemie began to see the shape of the pattern even though she couldn't hold all of it in her head at once. "It's like the light starts out meaning everything he wants," she said, drawing arrows on her chart. "Then later it starts to mean how the wanting itself might be the problem."

"Can a light convey all that?" Kaitlin asked. "It's a light. It conveys, like, green."

"It conveys whatever the writer keeps putting it near," said Noemie. "That's the trick. One symbol, wearing different coats."

Ms. Van Dijk from next door knocked at five, holding a package the mail carrier had left at the wrong house. "Ah," she said, peering at the poster board. "The 1925 Fitzgerald. I remember my landlord docked my deposit the year everyone in my building claimed to be reading it." She handed over the package and left them to it.

By dinner Noemie's chart had the green line running across every chapter, changing labels as it went. Noel looked at it and frowned. "So by the end, is the dream extinct, or just moved somewhere you can't reach it?"

Noemie uncapped the marker one more time and wrote both words, side by side, and let the question mark live between them.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: Paying only the minimum on a credit card means much of each payment goes to interest, so paying off the balance can take years.
story:
Clara pushed the calculator across the library table toward Calder. "Something's wrong with my mom's card," she said. "She pays every month, and the bill barely shrinks. I want to figure out why."

Calder leaned over the paper where Clara had copied the numbers from the bill her mom had left on the kitchen counter. The balance, the payment, and a small line marked "minimum payment" sat side by side. Clara had done the division twice already. "If she only pays the minimum, most of it seems to disappear somewhere," she said. "It doesn't come off the balance. It goes to interest."

"What's interest?" Calder asked.

"A fee for borrowing the money," Clara said. "But I keep thinking, if most of each payment goes to interest, then paying it all off could take years. That has to be it. She's paying the smallest amount allowed, so the big part never gets touched."

Ms. Eze passed their table on her way to the shelves and paused. "What's the project?"

"Not a project," Clara admitted. "A mystery." She showed the teacher the numbers, and Ms. Eze raised her eyebrows. "Test it," she said. "Make the payment bigger in your arithmetic and see what changes." She walked on before Clara could ask anything else.

So Clara tried it. She doubled the payment, and the balance dropped much faster, because a bigger share was actually striking the debt itself. Then she did the smallest payment again, and the years stacked up. "Look," she told Calder. "Same bill, same money owed. Only one number is different, and everything changes."

"That's not a very credible result," Calder said. "Nobody would design a bill that takes years to shrink."

"Maybe not on purpose," Clara said. She copied the two columns onto a fresh sheet to bring home.

That evening her mom read the paper twice, then got out her checkbook. "I'll pay more than the minimum this month," she said, "and every month after." She tapped the top column. "You did this with just a calculator?"

"And Calder," Clara said. "He didn't believe it either."

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: The least common denominator is the smallest number both denominators divide into evenly; for quarters and sixths it is 12.
story:
Daniel slid his worksheet across the table at math club and stared at the first problem: 1/4 plus 1/6. Around the room, kids were sharpening pencils, arguing quietly, and passing out crackers. Mr. Holloway had written one rule on the board: "Find a common denominator." That was all. No hints, no examples, and Daniel had a reputation for being the kid who finished these sheets first, which made the blank space at the top of his page feel like a dare.

Milla was already writing. She counted up by fours: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24. Then she counted by sixes: 6, 12, 18, 24. "Twenty-four," she announced. "Both of them go into twenty-four." She converted her fractions and got 6/24 plus 4/24 equals 10/24, then sat back looking satisfied.

Daniel tried to follow her, but something bothered him, like a sound in a wall he couldn't see behind. If 24 worked, maybe something smaller worked too. He couldn't see the answer directly, so he tested it the only way he could think of: he listed the multiples of four and the multiples of six and hunted for the first number sitting in both lines. Four, eight, twelve. Six, twelve. Twelve showed up in both, and earlier than 24 did. He wrote 3/12 plus 2/12 and got 5/12. Same answer as Milla, but with smaller numbers.

"Your way gives 10/24," Dexter said, leaning over from the next table after reading a note Daniel passed him. The note said: "Try 12. It's the smallest number both of them divide into evenly." Dexter looked at his own paper, crossed out his 24s, and rewrote everything. "Five-twelfths," he said. "Way less erasing."

Mr. Holloway walked by and paused at their table. "The smallest number both denominators divide into evenly is called the least common denominator," he said, and moved on before anyone could ask him anything else.

Milla frowned at her long column of numbers. "So I did extra work for nothing?" Daniel shrugged and turned his worksheet over. On the back he wrote a message and slid it to her: "Quarters and sixths go to twelve. Want to race the next one? Loser migrates to the cracker table." Milla read it, grinned, and flipped to the next problem. "You're going down," she said, pencil already moving.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: In 1977, scientists in the submersible Alvin found deep-sea vent communities whose food chains start with bacteria using chemicals from the vents, not sunlight.
story:
Eli crouched at the edge of Miller Pond with his science notebook, drawing arrows. Sun to algae, algae to snails, snails to a heron. "Boom," he said. "The whole pond, on one page."

"Your heron looks like a sock puppet," said Thorin, dropping down beside him.

"It's a top predator, Jax," Eli said, pointing, and Jax held up his hands like he'd been accused of a crime.

Then came the problem. Mr. Yamamoto, who was raking leaves by the pond's maple, leaned on his rake and said, "Good chain, Eli. Now tell me what happens if the snails vanish."

Eli stared at his arrows. "The heron gets hungry?"

"Get it wrong in an interesting way and you'll still learn something," Mr. Yamamoto said, and went back to raking.

The three of them tried it. Eli drew a big X over the snails and traced forward. The heron lost its lunch, sure. But then Jax flipped the notebook upside down and squinted at the algae. "If nothing eats these guys, do they just, like, take over the whole pond?" They watched the actual green scum along the shallows, giggling at the idea of algae excavating the pond like a construction crew, paving everything. Thorin spread his arms like a green canopy swallowing the sky. "Total algae empire."

That night Eli watched a documentary while eating cereal, and halfway through he froze, spoon in the air. Creatures were swimming around tall chimneys on the dark ocean floor, crabs and tube worms, thriving where no sunlight had ever reached. In 1977, scientists in a submersible called Alvin found whole communities down there, and the food chains started with bacteria using chemicals from the vents instead of sunlight.

The next morning he ran to the pond, notebook flapping. "Mr. Yamamoto! Not every food chain starts with the sun!" He showed his new drawing, arrows beginning at a wiggly blob labeled bacteria. "There are these vent places, totally dark, and it all starts with chemicals. That's radical."

Mr. Yamamoto set down his rake. "So if the vent disappeared?"

Eli grinned and drew one final arrow, straight down into nothing. "Everyone goes hungry. Sock puppet heron included."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food banks usually rotate stock by 'first in, first out', sending older items out before newer ones so less food expires on the shelves.
story:
Dylan had enrolled in the neighborhood cleanup mostly because Ray promised there would be donuts afterward, but when the crews split up, he and Yoan got assigned to the food bank on the corner instead of the park. The building smelled like cardboard and apples, and a volunteer was already dragging bags of trash out the back door from the cleanup that morning. "You two can stock shelves," the woman at the desk said, pointing to a crate of canned beans. Dylan grabbed armfuls and slid them onto the shelf at the front, right at eye level, where they looked tidy and easy to reach. He stood back, satisfied.

Then Mr. Rodríguez, who ran the food bank, walked past with a clipboard and stopped. "Nice work," he said, "but you'll have to move those to the back." Dylan stared at him. The cans at the front were the new ones, the shiniest ones, and he had lined them up like soldiers. "Why? They look better here."

"First in, first out," Mr. Rodríguez said, and hurried off toward the loading dock.

Dylan stood there, frowning. First in, first out. He looked at the shelf again and noticed something he had missed before: the older cans already sitting there had dust along their tops. That was the hidden pattern, the rule underneath the whole room. The older cans had arrived earlier, so they had to leave earlier, and the newer ones went behind them so less food expired on the shelves. The whole system ran backward from what he'd assumed, and the premise he'd started with, that new stuff goes in front, was exactly wrong.

He tested it. Starting at the canned fruit aisle, he checked every shelf, and sure enough, the dusty cans sat in front everywhere, the shiny ones behind. He tapped Yoan's shoulder. "New cans go in the back," he said. "Old ones up front. That's the whole trick."

They redid the beans together, sliding Dylan's shiny cans behind the dusty ones, then moved down the aisle pulling older soup to the front. An hour later Mr. Rodríguez came back, glanced down the row, and gave them a thumbs-up. "You figured it out," he called across the room.

Dylan grinned and pushed the last can into place.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: After about age 40, the lens of the eye loses flexibility and cannot focus up close as well, a condition called presbyopia that reading glasses correct.
story:
Edouard had spent all Saturday getting the guest bedroom ready, because Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. He had put fresh sheets on the bed, moved his model airplane off the dresser, and propped open the window so the room smelled like the lush garden below instead of like a closed-up box. When Grandpa arrived, he hugged Edouard so hard it seemed he was trying to compress him into a souvenir he could carry home.

The first morning, they walked to the market cafe on the corner. Grandpa ordered coffee, then picked up the menu and stretched his arm all the way out, tilting his head like he was trying to read a distant street sign. "Bigger print next time," he muttered, and asked the waitress to read the specials out loud. Edouard filed that away. At home, he noticed more: Grandpa held the newspaper at full arm's length, and when Edouard showed him a text message on his phone, Grandpa leaned back instead of forward, like the screen was a skunk.

Edouard remembered something from two summers ago, when his class had interviewed Mr. Sultani, the neighbour who ran the optical shop downtown. He couldn't remember the details, so that afternoon he searched through the drawer of his desk and found the thank-you letter Mr. Sultani had sent the class afterward. "Thank you for your thoughtful questions," he read to himself. "As I mentioned, after about age 40, the lens of the eye loses flexibility and cannot focus up close as well. The condition is called presbyopia, and reading glasses correct it." Edouard tapped the page. That was it. Grandpa was past 40 by a long shot, and everything he did fit the pattern: far away worked, close up did not. It was like a detective clue, and Edouard had a suspect.

Now he needed to test it. He wrote a secret message in tiny letters on a card and left it on the guest bedroom dresser. Then he left an identical message taped to the far wall in big letters. When Grandpa wandered in after lunch, Edouard said, "There's a hidden word somewhere in this room. First one to read it wins." Grandpa squinted at the little card, held it out, blinked, then laughed and turned straight to the wall. "RESILIENT," he read instantly. "I win. And you, young man, have set me up."

"Sort of," Edouard admitted. "It's the lens thing. Presbyopia, right? Mr. Sultani told our class." Grandpa sat down on the bed, still smiling. "Busted. I lost my reading glasses on the train, and I was too proud to say so all week." His voice dropped like it was a confession. "There's an optical shop two blocks over," Edouard said. "Belonging to the same Mr. Sultani."

They went the next morning. While Grandpa tried on frames, Edouard peeked at his own reflection and noticed he'd raised his hand to shield his eyes, a reflex he never knew he had. Grandpa picked a pair with wire rims, put them on, and picked up the smallest brochure on the counter. He read the first line out loud, clear as anything, then looked at Edouard over the top of the frames. "So," he said. "What else have you hidden around my room for me to find?"

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Squeezing or popping pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin and can leave scars.
story:
The mirror in the camp washhouse was small and spotted, but Piper could still see the red bump on her chin, right below her lip. Campfire Night was two days away, and the bump was not allowed.

She had been proud of herself all week. After the swim unit started, she'd noticed a pattern: on the days she skipped the showers because the water was cold, by afternoon she could smell herself, and so could everyone sitting near her at lunch. So she made a rule and stuck to it, even when the water made her yelp. Consistent showers, consistent deodorant, borrowed from her friend Yasmine until Piper's mom mailed her own. It had worked. The smell problem had dissolved like sugar in warm tea.

But the bump was new. She put two fingers on either side of it and pressed.

"Don't," said Yasmine, coming in with her towel. "My sister did that before the eighth-grade dance."

"Did what?"

"Squeezed it. Popped it." Yasmine set her shower caddy on the bench. "She told me popping pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin and can leave scars." She pointed at a small pale mark beside her own eyebrow. "That one's from when I was nine. I didn't listen either."

Piper looked at her fingers, still hovering near her chin. She thought about pushing something down into her skin instead of out of it. That seemed like exactly the wrong direction.

"So what do I do? Campfire Night is Friday."

"Wash it. Leave it alone. Cover it if you want. I have concealer." Yasmine held out a small tube. "Deklan's sister does theater, she taught him, and he showed me."

Friday evening, Piper sat beside the fire with a dab of concealer on her chin and her deodorant working quietly under her sleeves. Across the flames, Mr. Cruz was telling the story of the summer he won a soccer scholarship, and everyone was laughing at the part with the goose.

The bump was still there, smaller and unpopped, keeping its spot under the stars.

"Told you," Yasmine whispered.

Piper grinned and passed her the marshmallows.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final.
story:
Camille's grandfather jabbed his fork at the big screen above the booths. "Argentina won the first World Cup. Everybody knows that." Across the table, Killian shook his head so fast his hair flopped. "No way. My money's on Uruguay, and I want that chocolate cake if I'm right." Dessert was on the line, and nobody at the table had a phone, because the rule at Roma's was phones in the basket by the door until the match ended.

Camille wanted the cake too, but mostly she wanted the argument settled. On the wall near the kitchen hung a mural that portrayed a old-time football match, players in heavy shirts, a crowd on grassy banks. She had walked past it a dozen times without really looking. Now she looked. She stood up, crossed the room, and studied the painted scoreboard in the corner of the scene. It showed a final and a score, but the paint had faded where the winner's name should have been. She could make out a "4" and a "2" and nothing else.

"Checking my homework too?" said a voice. Ms. Brennan, the neighbour from the corner house, sat alone at the counter. She used to be a conductor on the river train before she retired, and she knew every regular in the place. Camille asked her straight out which country had won the first World Cup. "Uruguay," Ms. Brennan said. "Nineteen thirty. They beat Argentina four to two in the final." Camille ran through it once more in her head: first World Cup, Uruguay, 1930, four to two over Argentina. Then she asked Ms. Brennan to come say it to the table, because a mural and a memory were good, but a witness was better.

The grandpa leaned back, studied Ms. Brennan, and sighed. "Two slices of cake, then." Killian raised both arms like he had scored himself. Camille slid one plate in front of him and said, "Split it three ways, or I'm telling Grandpa you peeked at the mural first."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west.
story:
The plane touched down in Boston at seven in the morning, and Addison felt like a wet towel someone had wrung out. Two weeks ago, when her family had flown west to California for her aunt's wedding, she had stepped off the plane feeling perfectly fine, ready to swim in the hotel pool before lunch. Now her eyes burned, her head ached, and the airport lights seemed too bright. Her dad steered the luggage cart toward baggage claim while Addison shuffled behind him like a zombie.

At the carousel she slumped into a plastic chair beside a boy from their flight who was rubbing his eyes too. "I slept on the plane," he said, "and I still feel like a melted candle." Across the aisle, a family with three kids was waiting for a flight going west, and those kids were bouncing around a vending machine, wide awake, arguing loudly about chips. Addison stared at them, then at the boy, then at the departures board. The pattern began to condense in her mind: everyone here heading east looked exhausted, and everyone heading west looked fine. She remembered that going out had been easy too, and that was also westward.

Her objective now was simple: prove it. She walked up and down the gate area, quietly watching faces. A woman napping against a pillar held a boarding pass for Denver. Two energetic teenagers were checking in for a Seattle flight. Every droopy person, without exception, was eastbound.

By the time her dad pulled their suitcase off the belt, she had counted eleven travelers, and the pattern held every single time. She followed him toward the exit, yawning, and decided she would test it again on the next trip, if they ever flew somewhere east first, just to be sure. Outside, the morning air was cold and sharp.

"Hey, Dad," she said, climbing into the taxi, "when we fly west, can I get the window seat?"

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: A topic is a subject a novel is about, such as friendship, while a theme is a full statement of what the novel says about that subject.
story:
The bus lurched around the corner by the bakery, and Emily grabbed the seat in front of her with both hands. "I got it back," she said, digging into her backpack. "My theme worksheet. Mr. Kang graded it."

Lilith leaned over the aisle. "And?"

"Two out of ten." Emily smoothed the crumpled paper on her knees. "I wrote that the theme of The Sea Cage is friendship, and he circled it and wrote one word. See?"

Willa squinted at it. "It says 'closer.' That's it? Closer?"

"That's it." Emily flopped back against the window. "The book club meets at lunch and I'm supposed to lead the theme discussion. If I can't even get a theme right, Willa, I'm going to stand there like a seaweed."

"Okay," said Lilith, in her calm way that meant she was about to intervene whether Emily wanted her to or not. "Read me the exact definition off the board. You copied it down, right? You copy everything down, including the fire drill schedule."

Emily flipped to the back of her notebook and found it. "'A topic is a subject a novel is about, such as friendship. A theme is a full statement of what the novel says about that subject.'"

The bus rattled over the tracks. Willa counted on her fingers. "So friendship is the topic. That's the subject. But a theme is a whole statement, like a sentence, about what the book actually says about friendship."

"So the theme can't just be one word," Emily said slowly. "It has to say something." She sat up so fast she banged her elbow on the window. "Ow. Okay, ow, but listen. The Sea Cage says friendship survives even when people are separated. There's that part where Marek sends a message in a bottle and it takes a year to arrive and Dory waits anyway. That's the book saying something about friendship. That's a statement."

"Back it up," said Lilith. "Mr. Kang always wants a quotation."

Emily found the page, already soft from being read eleven times. "'A cage can hold a body, but it cannot hold a promise.' Page one forty-three."

Willa grinned. "Say it louder, the whole bus should hear that."

Emily said it louder. A seventh grader two seats back looked over, then gave her a thumbs up for reasons nobody understood, and the three of them cracked up until the driver glanced in the mirror.

At the next stop Emily borrowed Lilith's pen and wrote on the back of the worksheet, right under Mr. Kang's lonely word: "Theme: The Sea Cage says that true friendship endures separation. Quotation: 'A cage can hold a body, but it cannot hold a promise,' p. 143." She felt strangely buoyant, like the worksheet itself might float out of her hands and sail to school ahead of the bus.

"You realize," said Willa, "that in the book, the message went by sea. You're about to deliver yours by Mr. Kang. Slightly faster."

"Vastly faster," said Emily. "The hierarchy of message delivery. Bottle, pigeon, teacher."

At the front doors she stepped off first, worksheet held flat like a tray of something that might spill, and marched straight down the hall toward room twelve.

"Mr. Kang," she called, "one more try before lunch?"

activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
knowledge_domain: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
fact: Actors split a script into beats: a new beat starts wherever a character's thought or tactic changes, and a pause often marks that shift.
story:
Savannah's pencil hovered over her script until Alana grabbed it and snapped a piece off for herself. They were sprawled on the saggy velvet seats of the community theatre, an hour before rehearsal, and both of them had the same problem: the monologue from Ms. Wanjiru's play had to be memorized by Friday.

"I keep rushing," Savannah said. "When I performed it Tuesday, Ms. Wanjiru said it sounded like I was reciting a grocery list." She smoothed the crumpled page on her knee. The monologue belonged to a girl who was deciding whether to tell her best friend a secret that could break their friendship. Every time Savannah practiced, she charged straight through it, and the part where the girl changes her mind came out flat.

Alana was drawing slashes in her margin. "Violette showed me this. Watch." She tapped the page. "You split it into beats. A new beat starts wherever your character's thought or tactic changes. You put a slash there." She drew one after "I should tell her" and another after "No. Not yet." "Then when you get to a slash, you stop. You breathe. Violette says the pause marks the shift."

Savannah studied Alana's slashes. Something clicked, the way a code clicks. "So the girl's first thought is, my friend deserves the truth. That's one beat. Then her thought changes to, but I'll lose her. That's a new beat." She started penciling slashes of her own, hunting for each place where the girl switched tactics, first pleading, then justifying, then almost deciding to abandon the whole plan and keep quiet forever. "It's like the pauses are invisible," she said. "Nobody in the audience sees the slashes, but they'd feel them."

When rehearsal started, Savannah stood on the mark under the hot stage lights and let the first slash do its work. "I should tell her." Pause. She let her hands drop instead of waving them around, because the stillness felt louder than a gesture ever had. Ms. Wanjiru leaned forward in the third row. Down in the front row, Violette whispered something to Alana that might have been praise and might have been something else, ambiguous in the dark, but Savannah didn't try to figure it out. She hit the last slash, the one where the girl finally decides, and stopped breathing entirely for two seconds.

"Better," Ms. Wanjiru called up. "Much better. But you missed a beat. Right there, after 'she'd never forgive me.' Her thought changes there too. Find it, mark it."

Savannah flipped her script over, found the line, and pressed her pencil down hard enough to leave a dent. "One more slash," she said, and stepped back onto her mark.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator; some small animals survive winter in tunnels under the snow.
story:
Sophia heard the news at 6:47 in the morning, when her dad burst into her room shouting "Snow day!" and the whole world outside her window had turned white and impossible. By eight she was dragging her sled up the hill behind the school, where Ally was already waiting with two thermoses and a plan.

"Fort first," Ally said, pointing at the deep drift near the fence. "I want one with a roof this time. Last year's fell in before lunch." Ally's little brother had laughed at that fort for a week, so this one had to be perfect.

They cut blocks with the green plastic shovel and stacked them in a ring, then leaned slabs across the top. Sophia squeezed inside first. The wind that had been biting her ears all morning went silent, and the air felt strange, almost mild, like a different room. She scrutinized the walls, pressing her mittened hand against the lumpy white blocks. Outside, her fingers ached. Inside, they stopped aching.

"Come feel this," she called. Ally ducked in, and her eyebrows shot up. "It's warmer in here. That's so weird. Snow is frozen, so how is it warm?"

Sophia thought about the snow itself, the way it piled up light and fluffy instead of solid like ice. "It's mostly air, I think," she said slowly. "All that fluff, it's like a blanket. A blanket is mostly air too." She remembered a page from the nature book on her nightstand, and it clicked. "That's how little animals make it through winter. They live in tunnels under the snow. The snow keeps them warm."

"That's the best fact I've ever heard," Ally whispered, like they had discovered a secret the hill had been keeping all along. They dug a small side chamber with the shovel, just to see how quiet and cozy a tunnel could be.

Jayda arrived at noon with her saucer and her usual need for speed, and she wasted no time. "Fort? Boring. Racing? Yes." She beat Sophia three times down the steepest run, cutting agile turns around the spot where a rock hid under the white, and Sophia beat her twice on the slower side path where the snow was packed hard and fast. Then Jayda came off the hill for cocoa and, out of pure curiosity, stuck her head inside the fort.

"Whoa," she said, and did not come out for ten minutes. "I'm spending the night here. Seriously. I'm bringing a sleeping bag."

"You'll freeze by midnight," Ally said.

"Will not," said Sophia. "That's the whole point of the fort."

They stared at each other, and the twist arrived in Jayda's grin. "Then prove it. Thermometer. Tonight."

At dinner Sophia found the outdoor thermometer in the junk drawer and held it up like a trophy. Her dad asked what it was for, and she only smiled. Tomorrow she would show Ally and Jayda the numbers, and in the meantime she turned the little dial over and over in her hands.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
The group chat pinged at 7:04, right after dinner, while Harper was still clearing her plate. It was Waylon, posting a screenshot of the school basketball stats page. Under "Field Goal Percentage," one name glowed at the top of the ranking: Brent, 100 percent. Below him, everyone else clustered in the twenties and thirties. Waylon wrote, "Brent is officially a machine. Unbeatable."

Brent jumped in fast. "Told you guys. Perfect season. Best shooter on the team, no debate."

Harper frowned at her phone. She had been at every game. She tried to picture Brent shooting, and the picture would not come. She scrolled back through the chat, then put the phone down, finished drying the dish she was holding, and picked it up again. She typed, "How many shots have you taken total?" and hit send before she could talk herself out of it.

"Doesn't matter," Brent answered. "The stat says what it says."

Harper pulled up the same stats page on her laptop. She found the column she actually wanted, the one nobody ever reposted: attempts. There it was. Brent had taken one shot all season. He had made it, in the fourth quarter of a game that was already decided, and one make out of one attempt came out to 100 percent on the page. Meanwhile their teammate who had taken forty shots and made eighteen sat near the bottom of the ranking at 45 percent, which was, Harper thought, genuinely bizarre. The ranking made it look like Brent was twice as good, when really he had barely played.

She did not want to embarrass him in front of everyone, so she sent him one private message instead. "Cool shot. But 100 percent on one shot just means one for one. Take ten more and see what happens." She watched the typing dots appear, vanish, appear again. Finally a reply came: "Fair. Ask coach to put me in Friday."

Friday night, the gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn. Brent got real minutes for the first time. He took six shots and made two, and by the end his percentage on the season had dropped below the teammate everyone had scrolled past. After the buzzer, Waylon started a new chat called "The Treaty of Honest Stats," where everyone agreed to post attempts next to percentages from now on, because a ranking without the attempts could quietly deteriorate into nonsense by the end of a season. Brent was the first to sign it.

He jogged over to Harper by the water fountain, ball under his arm. "Two for seven," he said. "Worst 100 percent I ever had."

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: Stage fright is the body's fight-or-flight response: adrenaline can cause a racing heart, a dry mouth, a shaky voice and trembling hands.
story:
Brielle stood in the wings with her flute clutched against her chest, and her hands would not stop trembling. Not a little wobble, but a full shake, like her fingers had opinions of their own. Her heart pounded so hard she could hear it, her mouth had gone dry as chalk, and when she tried a quiet note, her voice came out shaky. Which was ridiculous, because her hands were supposed to be the problem, not her voice, and she was only talking to Tanya.

"Look at them," Tanya whispered, holding out her own fingers. They fluttered like nervous little birds. "Why is this happening? We've practiced this piece a hundred times."

Brielle scrutinized her friend's hands, then her own, wondering. Something invisible was doing this to both of them, and it wasn't nerves exactly, because they weren't even scared of the music anymore. Then she remembered the library book from last month. In her flashback, she was sprawled on the rug at home, reading about how every organism, from a rabbit to a person, has something called fight-or-flight, and how adrenaline floods the body and can cause a racing heart, a dry mouth, a shaky voice and trembling hands. The rabbit wasn't broken when it trembled before running. It was getting ready.

"Adrenaline," Brielle said out loud. "It's fight-or-flight. Our bodies think we're about to have to run for our lives, so they're getting everything ready. That's all this is."

Tanya stared at her. "So we're not falling apart?"

"We're warming up." Brielle had a simple idea, and she wanted to test it. If the shaking was leftover running energy, maybe she could burn some of it off before the curtain. She put down her flute, rolled her shoulders, and shook her hands hard, like she was flicking water off them. "Try it. Tell your body, okay, you got the message, now use it."

Tanya laughed and copied her, and for a moment the two of them looked like windmills in the wings. Brielle's heart still hammered, but when she picked up her flute, her fingers were steadier. She sipped from her water bottle, and her mouth wasn't quite so dry.

Ms. Banerjee's voice floated from the stage. "And now, our flute duo, Brielle and Tanya!"

They walked out. The lights were hot and white, and Brielle felt one last flutter in her stomach, but her hands stayed quiet on the keys. She lifted the flute, glanced sideways at Tanya, and whispered, "Ready to run?"

"Ready to fly," Tanya whispered back.

The first note rang out, clear and true.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: A frost, hailstorm or drought that ruins part of a strawberry crop reduces the supply, which pushes the price of the remaining berries up.
story:
Emilie stacked the pint baskets in a neat pyramid while Mr. Weiss taped a new sign to the front of the farm stand. The sign said five dollars a pint, and last week it had said three. She could smell the warm, sweet berries even through the porous weave of the baskets, the little holes that let air move through so the fruit would not spoil.

"That's way too much," said Joelle, poking the sign with one finger. "I only brought four dollars."

"A late frost got half the field," Emilie said. She pointed across the road, where one long row of plants stood brown and limp next to rows that were green and full. "Those plants that flourished before the frost, they're all we've got left. Mr. Weiss says fewer berries means the price has to go up, or he loses money on the whole season." She was still figuring out exactly how that worked, but she had a plan to test it.

When Joelle walked off toward the bus stop with her empty hands, Emilie flipped the stand's little notebook to the page where Mr. Weiss wrote the winter prices. In February, when the berries came from far away in trucks, a pint had cost seven dollars, and in July, when the whole field dripped with fruit, it had cost two. She drew three columns: how many berries, what season, what price. The pattern jumped right off the page, like a picture of something she could not see directly. Fewer berries, higher price. More berries, lower price. The frost had not touched the price sign; it had touched the field, and the field had touched the sign.

"Emilie, customer," Mr. Weiss called. A woman stood at the counter with a little boy, a family who had arrived from the city last month, and the boy was staring at the strawberries the way Joelle stared at puppies.

"They're five dollars today," Emilie said, and then, remembering her columns, she added, "but there'll be a bigger picking in two weeks, and they should get cheaper then."

"Then we'll come back in two weeks," the woman said, and the boy grinned and waved goodbye all the way to their car.

Emilie wrote five dollars in the notebook, and beside it, in small careful letters, two weeks: lower.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the United States, the cost of crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so pump prices tend to rise when crude oil prices rise.
story:
Sawyer had forty-one dollars saved, and the green mountain bike on the marketplace app cost sixty. Every night after dinner he opened the app and checked the listing. The bike had been sixty dollars for two weeks. Then three people asked about it on the same afternoon, and by morning the seller had raised the price to ninety-five.

"Ninety-five!" Sawyer said at school the next day. He showed Jocelyn and Izaiah the screen. "It went up because everybody wants it. There's only one."

"So wait until nobody wants it," Jocelyn said, like it was obvious. Izaiah shook his head. "Then somebody else buys it. That's the whole problem."

On the walk home, Sawyer stopped at Mr. Sultani's gas station to buy a carbohydrate bar with his last crumpled dollar, because walking everywhere made him hungry. A kid at the pumps was tugging his dad's sleeve. "Why is it more than last week?" the kid asked, pointing at the big numbers on the sign.

Mr. Sultani was wiping the pump handle, and he answered without looking up. "Crude oil went up. Crude oil is usually the biggest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so when it rises, my prices rise too." Sawyer stared at the sign. So the numbers weren't magic. Something far away, something he couldn't see, was pulling them up, the same way invisible buyers pulled up the bike's price. He asked Mr. Sultani one more question on the way out. "So if crude oil falls, does the pump price fall?" Mr. Sultani nodded. "Usually it comes back down."

That gave Sawyer an idea, and ideas were something his mother called his most fertile quality, like good soil where things grew whether he wanted them to or not. He couldn't make crude oil fall. But he could test the rule on the bike. First he needed money, and the only thing he owned that anyone wanted was his set of snow-tiger cards. Only six were printed with the blue stripe, and last month nobody had cared. He checked the marketplace and found five buyers asking in a single day. Scarce, plus many people wanting it. He listed the cards that night and watched three bids push the price from eight dollars to twenty-two.

By Saturday he had enough to offer the seller sixty for the bike, but with a message: "I can pay today." The seller wrote back that two of the three interested buyers had vanished, and since the bike had been sitting in his garage all winter like a bear trying to hibernate, sixty worked for him. Sawyer rode home with the wind in his face, and when he passed the station he slowed down just to see the numbers on the sign. They had dropped six cents. He grinned and rang his bell.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: You can check an answer to an equation by putting it back in place of the variable; if both sides come out equal, the answer is right.
story:
The bell over the door jangled as Quinn pushed into Mr. Gallagher's corner store, her math binder clamped under one arm. She set it on the counter beside the register, next to the jar of pickled eggs, and slid her homework across the glass. "Can I sit in the back booth while my mom picks up my brother? It's just for twenty minutes."

"Booth's yours," said Mr. Gallagher, who let kids do their homework there as long as they bought something. Quinn paid for a bag of pretzels and carried the binder to the booth by the ice machine.

The worksheet had six equations, and five of them were done. The sixth was 2x plus 3 equals 11, and under it she was supposed to plot the line on the coordinate grid at the bottom of the page. Quinn had written x equals 4, because half of 8 was 4, but something about it felt shaky. She had subtracted 3 from both sides first, then divided, and she was almost sure the order was right, but almost was not the same as sure. Her grandfather checked her homework every night, and last Tuesday he had circled a whole column in red pencil. The guilt from that still sat in her stomach whenever she hesitated over a number.

She stared at the problem, chewing a pretzel. Then she had an idea. If x really was 4, she could put it back where the x had been and see what happened. She wrote 2 times 4 plus 3. Two times 4 was 8, and 8 plus 3 was 11. The left side came out to 11, exactly what the right side said. Both sides matched, so 4 had to be right. She sat back, surprised at how simple it had been, like testing a key in a lock instead of guessing whether it fit.

The door jangled again and Gwendolyn came in, scarf still on, heading straight for the booth. "Mr. Gallagher said you were drowning in math back here."

"Actually, I think I just figured something out." Quinn slid the paper across. "Watch. I solved this one and got 4. But I wasn't sure, so I put the 4 back in place of the x. Two times 4 plus 3 is 11, and the other side is 11 too. If both sides come out equal, the answer's right."

Gwendolyn pulled out her own worksheet, the same one, and frowned at her first problem. "I got x equals 5 on this one, but I rushed." She tried 5 in place of the variable, worked it through with her finger under each number, and her shoulders dropped. "They don't match. I have to redo it."

"Do it here," Quinn said, and nudged the pretzels across the table.

They worked side by side, meticulous with every sign, and when Gwendolyn's new answer finally made both sides equal, she drew the point on the grid and started the line through it with a ruler borrowed from Mr. Gallagher's pencil cup. The line climbed steadily across the page, tidy and certain, depicting every answer the equation could ever give.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Age-related hearing loss usually affects high-pitched sounds first, so voices can sound muffled even when they are loud enough.
story:
Grandpa Frank had been at the house for three days, and every trip to Willow Park went the same way. Laurence would say something, he would turn his head toward her with that polite, blank smile, and she would repeat it louder, and louder again, until half the park turned to look.

"There's something wrong with my pattern of thinking," she told Maria on the benches by the duck pond. Maria raised one eyebrow with total skepticism, so Laurence laid it out. "He hears me. He knows I'm talking. But he misses the words. If he were going deaf, loud wouldn't help at all. But loud does help a little, which means it's not only about loudness. Something else is the problem, and I can't see it directly."

"So test it," Maria said, reasonably.

Grandpa Frank was feeding the ducks, tossing bread in slow arcs. Laurence marched over and ran her experiment. She whispered something in her normal, high voice, close to his ear. He leaned in and missed it. Then she dropped her voice as low as she could make it, still whispering, and said the exact same sentence. "Grandpa, the ducks are plotting something." He laughed out loud.

"Plotting, are they? Well, tell them to get in line behind your grandmother."

Laurence's whole face went warm with the discovery. It wasn't volume. When she spoke low, the words landed. When she spoke high, they turned muffled even though she was loud enough. Somewhere in her mind a piece clicked into place, as fundamental as a key in its own lock, and she thought she understood: his ears must catch some sounds fine and lose others, the low ones arriving whole while the high ones went missing.

Mr. Delgado, the retired teacher who played chess at the stone tables, had been watching from under his sun hat. "You figured out what took my sister two years and a doctor," he said. "Same thing happens to me."

On the walk home, Laurence practiced keeping her voice low and slow, like a radio announcer. At the gate Grandpa Frank stopped and squinted at her.

"You've changed how you talk," he said. "Why?"

She hadn't planned to admit it. "Because when I go high, you miss my words. So I'm staying low."

He was quiet while a sparrow swooped for the last crumbs in his pocket. Then he took her hand, which he hadn't done once all week, and said, "Then let's get you a megaphone, for emergencies only."

"Deal," Laurence said, low and clear.

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: A swimmer's head pushes a bow wave that leaves a dip in the water beside the face, letting the mouth reach air below the level of the flat surface.
story:
Eli stood at the shallow end of the community pool, gripping the wall and watching the lanes. He had to swim twenty-five metres of front crawl with side breathing before summer ended, and so far he had made it exactly eight metres before choking on water. Joshua had already passed the test on Monday. "You lift your whole head out," Joshua said, treading water beside him. "That's why you sink. Ms. Charles says keep your cheek on the water." Eli nodded, but he didn't believe it. How could you breathe if your face stayed down there, where the water was?

He pushed off and tried again. Three strokes, then he hauled his face upward, high and desperate, and his legs dropped like stones. He came up spluttering. The chlorine stung his eyes, sharp and almost corrosive, and he wiped them on his shoulder. At the far end, Ms. Charles walked the deck in her slow loop, orbiting the pool the way she always did, watching every lane at once.

Joshua waited for him at the wall. "Want to see something weird?" He put his face in the water right beside Eli, blew bubbles, and turned his head just a little. "Look at the edge of my face," he said between breaths. Eli leaned in. Where Joshua's cheek cut through the water, a small wave piled up in front of his head, and right behind that wave, beside his mouth, the surface dipped lower than the flat water everywhere else. In that little dip, Joshua's mouth was finding air even though his face was barely turned at all.

"That's not possible," Eli said. "Your mouth is below the water line." But he had seen it. His head pushes a wave out ahead of it, and that wave leaves a pocket behind it, a hollow beside the face, and that's where the air is. The water wasn't one flat level like he'd imagined. It was a shape that his own head made.

He set off again. This time he kept one goggle in the water and turned his head only as far as his shoulder. The wave rose in front of his forehead, the dip opened beside his mouth, and he caught a breath of real air without lifting anything. Stroke, stroke, breathe. Stroke, stroke, breathe. The flags overhead passed, then the rope that divided the lanes. His arms burned and his rhythm wobbled once near the deep end, but he thought about nothing except the little pocket waiting beside his face each time.

His hand slapped the far wall. Twenty-five metres. He turned around, breathless and grinning, and Joshua was already shouting from the shallow end. "Told you!" Eli laughed and spat a mouthful of pool water toward the gutter. "I'm probably drinking a million microbes a lap," he called back, "and I don't even care." Ms. Charles raised her clipboard from the side of the deck and wrote something down.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In the United States, a permanent change of address filed with the Postal Service forwards First-Class Mail to the new address for 12 months.
story:
Scarlett sat in the back row of Room 12 with her hands folded, waiting for Mr. Vogel to finish attendance so she could stop being the new kid. Her parents had filed the change of address form two weeks ago, on the same day the movers carried out her dresser and her cat's scratching post. At her old school, she and Shreya had made a deal: real letters, because Shreya's handwriting was too good to waste on texts. Scarlett had already mailed one from Ohio with a drawing of her new street on the back.

Three days later, a thick envelope appeared on the kitchen counter. Her mom slid it over. "This came for you. Old address, but somebody forwarded it."

Scarlett studied the sticker. Her own old street number was crossed out in marker, and underneath was this one, printed small and neat. Shreya's letter had followed her across two states. Scarlett turned the envelope over twice, thinking. It hadn't been luck. Something in the postal system must hold on to the old address and resend things for a while. She wanted to know how long, so she typed it into the library computer before school.
