"Forwards First-Class Mail for twelve months," she whispered. A whole year. That was her window. After that, Shreya's letters would pile up in some dead-letter bin, unless everyone had the new address by then.

On Monday, she brought the envelope to show Mr. Vogel during homeroom. "My friend's letter found me," she said. "The forwarding runs out next August, so I'm going to make sure every single person has my address way before that."

"Smart premise," said Mr. Vogel, tapping her sticker. "You've discovered the Postal Service's most resilient trick."

The boy in front of her, Joaquin, turned around. "Wait, mail follows you? I thought it just, like, gave up."

"Joaquin, mail never gives up," Scarlett said. She spread Shreya's three pages across her desk, and Joaquin leaned back to read the part about the hamster.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Frost-tender crops such as tomatoes, peppers and squash are planted outdoors only after the last spring frost, because freezing temperatures kill them.
story:
Jace had planted his tomato seedlings three weeks early because he wanted the first ripe tomato on the block before Johnathan got one. Now the evening news said tonight would drop below freezing, and freezing temperatures kill tomatoes, peppers and squash, plants that can only go outside after the last spring frost. Jace stood in the backyard with his hands in his pockets, staring at the six little green rows he was so proud of.

He thought about the way frost worked. It settled on open leaves, but it could not settle on something covered. He couldn't see cold air moving through the yard, but he could test his idea the way Mr. Harper, his neighbour, tested things: one thing covered, one thing not. He grabbed two buckets and set one over a seedling, then left the plant beside it bare. "That's my experiment," he told Desmond, who had climbed over the fence to see what was going on.

"It seems trivial," Desmond said, "covering one plant."

"It's not trivial to the plant," Jace said. He looked at the rest of the rows and knew the buckets wouldn't stretch that far. Desmond noticed him counting and ran home for old bedsheets, and Johnathan showed up with his little brother's tent poles. The three of them draped sheets over every seedling and pinned them down with stones, revising the plan twice when the wind kept lifting a corner near the fence.

The morning was white and stiff with cold. Jace pulled off the buckets and sheets one by one, holding his breath. The uncovered test plant was slumped and dark, but under the covers, every seedling stood green. Desmond whooped, and Johnathan patted the bucket-covered plant like it was a lucky tenant that had rented the safest room in the yard.

Mr. Harper leaned over the fence with his coffee. "So," he said. "What did the experiment tell you?"

"Covered plants made it," Jace said. "And I'm never planting before the last frost again." He picked up the empty bucket and turned it upside down to dry in the sun.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The core shadow is the darkest band of shadow on the sphere itself, lying just past the terminator on the side away from the light.
story:
Victor sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with a pencil, an orange, and the desk lamp pulled close. He had promised Ms. Moose he would practice shading before Monday's art class, and Grandpa's house was the quietest place to do it. He propped the orange on a folded napkin and switched on the lamp, watching how the light made a small bright spot on one side and let the other side fall into grey. How dark was dark, though? Where did the light actually stop?

He shaded the whole dark side the same even grey, then held the page up next to the orange. His drawing looked like a flat disc someone had cut from paper. The orange on the napkin did not look like that at all. Victor squinted at it, turning his head. The darkest part was not at the very edge, he noticed. It was a band a little past where the light ran out, on the far side. He wondered if his pencil could find that. He rubbed his shading darker in just that band, then let the far edge go lighter again, faint and round. The sphere popped off the page. He actually said "whoa" out loud, alone in the kitchen.

The doorbell rang. Yousuf had biked over, sketchbook under his arm, sniffing from an acute allergy attack because Grandpa kept a cat. "I keep messing mine up," Yousuf said, showing a page of flat grey circles. "Ms. Moose will think I drew coins."

"Put your eraser away and look at this first," Victor said, holding up the orange. "Where's the darkest part?" Yousuf pointed at the far edge. Victor shook his head and traced a curve in the air, a little past the bright side's ending, on the side away from the lamp. "There. It's a band. Grandpa called it the core shadow when he saw my practice sheet."

"Grandpa draws?"

"He went to art school for a year. He never mentioned it before today."

Grandpa came in with lemonade and two cookies, and began to nurture their little drawings with careful, approving nods. He looked at Yousuf's page, picked up the pencil, and said, "Same grey on the whole side won't give you a ball. Now try it, son. Band first, edge last."

Yousuf leaned in and started to draw.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is marked by lighting small oil lamps called diyas and is usually celebrated over five days.
story:
Zoe knelt on the grass near the park pavilion, setting out small clay lamps in a neat row along the ledge where her grandmother's table met the window of the rental shelter. Grandmother called the lamps diyas, and she had promised to light them at dusk. "Five days of Diwali," Grandmother had said that morning, "so tonight is only the beginning." Zoe counted the lamps twice. Fourteen on the ledge, but she had made sixteen.

She looked around the pavilion. Ms. Jean-Louis, who taught science at her school and had come with a plate of sweets, was chatting with a man in an orange scarf. Thalia and Orlando were stacking paper cups by the lemonade. Nobody near the table. Zoe tried to classify the possibilities: someone borrowed two lamps, she had miscounted the box, or the lamps had never made it out of the car. Miscounting was the boring answer, so she checked the box. Empty, with crinkly paper lining the bottom.

Then she noticed something odd, almost a paradox: the paper cups were moving. Orlando's neat tower leaned and collapsed all by itself. Zoe watched the cups slide sideways in a slow little herd. Wind, she thought, but the trees beyond the pavilion hung perfectly still. She crouched and held a scrap of napkin near the ledge. It fluttered hard. The wind was squeezing between the pavilion's back wall and the tall hedge, like water through a narrowed hose, and only there.

"Grandmother!" Zoe called. "The lamps will blow out, and two already rolled off the ledge into the hedge. Can we move them to the front rail?" Grandmother came over, squinted at the napkin fluttering like an eccentric little flag, and laughed. "You found the sneaky wind. Yes, clever one, the front rail." Together they carried the diyas one by one, and Zoe lined them up facing the pond, where the air was calm. Thalia jogged over, cupping a rescued lamp in both hands. "Found these two in the bushes. They're a bit grassy." "Perfect," Zoe said. "Grassy diyas. Front rail, end of the line."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: In his Rhetoric, the Greek philosopher Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, logic and evidence.
story:
Brielle sat at her grandfather's kitchen table with her essay notes spread out like a battle plan. Mr. Rahman had made the assignment mandatory for the whole class: a five-paragraph persuasive essay, with an introduction, three body paragraphs, and a conclusion. She had the structure. What she didn't have was a clue how to actually persuade anyone of anything. She wanted to argue that the school should let fifth graders use the community garden plot that sat empty behind the fence. She just couldn't figure out why anyone would listen to her.

"You look like a person arguing with a blank page," her grandfather said, setting down two mugs of cocoa.

"I have to write something convincing," Brielle said. "Shaun says convincing people is just luck. Aria says it's about being loud." She frowned at her notes. "They can't both be right, and I don't think either of them is."

Her grandfather leaned over and tapped a word she had scribbled in the margin: PATHOS. "Where did you pick up that Greek?"

Brielle blinked. "It's not Greek. It's... actually, I don't know what it is. I heard the word somewhere and it sounded good." She flipped her pencil over and erased it, then wrote it again, because something about it still felt important.

"Two thousand years ago a philosopher named Aristotle wrote the Rhetoric," her grandfather said. "He was my favorite troublemaker when I was in school. Go look on the second shelf, the fat blue book with the cracked spine." Brielle found it, dusty and heavier than it looked, and brought it to the table. He opened it to a marked page. "He described three ways to persuade. One of them is ethos."

"Ethos," she repeated slowly.

"That's the speaker's credibility," her grandfather said. "Whether people believe you're worth hearing."

Brielle read the page twice, her lips moving. Then she grabbed a fresh sheet and drew three columns. At the top of the first she wrote ETHOS, and under it: I have grown tomatoes on the balcony for two years. I know soil goes sour when nobody touches it. At the top of the second she wrote PATHOS, and under it: the garden looks lonely in autumn, and the whole class walks past it every single day. The third column took longer, but she wrote LOGOS and under it: studies of school gardens, empty plot costs the school nothing, weeding is free labor. Logic and evidence, she thought, that one has to be logos.

She tested the idea on her grandfather the way she planned to test it on paper. "Grandpa, may I have the last cookie?" she asked, pointing at the ethos column. "I'm the one who baked them, so I know they won't burn anybody." He shook his head, grinning. She tried again with pathos, describing how she'd been saving that cookie all afternoon and how sad the empty plate would make her. He laughed out loud and broke it in half. "Three tries, three ways," she said, writing quickly. "It works."

By the time her cocoa had gone cold, she had a full introduction drafted and one body paragraph about ethos that Mr. Rahman would probably underline. Her grandfather read over her shoulder, then pointed at a sentence about Aristotle. "You know," he said, "you're not the first person in this family to argue with that book. It helped my father's letters thrive when he wrote to the government about the old neighborhood. Every descendant in this house has owed that old Greek something." Brielle looked at her three columns, then at the fat blue book, and pulled it closer to her side of the table.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: The bandwagon fallacy claims something must be right or good simply because many people believe it or do it.
story:
Dominic sat at the kitchen table with his essay packet flattened in front of him. The assignment was a five-paragraph persuasive essay, one introduction, three reasons, one conclusion, and he already knew his topic: why his family should get a dog. He narrated his plan out loud while he wrote, because talking it through made the words come faster. Reason one was his strongest, he thought. He underlined it twice. Everyone at school has a dog, so dogs must be good pets.

That evening he called Mustafa to read him the draft. "Paragraph two is the best part," Dominic said. "Everyone at school wants one. Even kids on the affluent street behind the school, the ones with the big yards, they all have two dogs each. So it must be the right thing to do."

There was a pause on the line, long enough that Dominic checked whether the call had dropped. "Mr. Çelik marked that off my essay last week," Mustafa said slowly. "It's called the bandwagon fallacy. He circled it in red because I wrote that something must be good just because many people believe it or do it." Dominic argued for a minute, then hung up and stared at his underlined sentence. If the reason was broken, his whole essay leaned on a cracked leg.

He decided to test it. The next day he asked around, keeping a tally in the margin of his notebook. Danny, it turned out, was allergic and had never had a dog at all. Two kids in his row had cats. When he counted, more than half the class had no dog. His strongest reason wasn't just weak, it wasn't even true. Dominic sat with that for a while, tapping his pencil. If everyone-owns-one couldn't hold up paragraph two, he needed a reason that could.

Then it hit him, and the hit stung a little. He didn't want a dog because everyone had one. He wanted a dog because of the old spaniel next door, the one he had helped care for last spring, holding her still while his neighbour gave her the antibiotic for her bad tooth, walking her slowly down the driveway on warm afternoons. She had been gentle in a way that no tally or count could measure. Nobody else even knew about her.

He crossed out his underlined sentence and wrote a new paragraph two about a dog who had trusted a ten-year-old with her medicine and her slow walks. When his mother leaned over his shoulder at the table, she read it twice and set down her tea. "Get your shoes on," she said. "The shelter closes at six."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snowflakes almost always have six sides or six arms, because water molecules link together in a six-sided pattern when they freeze.
story:
The radio announced it at six in the morning, and Maya ran to the window in her pajamas to see for herself. Snow. A whole white plateau of it covering the backyard, with more coming down in fat, unhurried flakes. No school. She ate her cereal fast, texted Alexe, who lived three streets over and had already shoveled his front walk twice just for fun, and then she pulled on her boots, her coat, and her grandmother's dark wool mitten, the black one with the snowflake pattern stitched around the cuff.

She had a question, and she meant to answer it. Yesterday in science, Mr. Katz had put a photograph of a single snowflake on the board and said, "Look closely. Count." Maya had counted six arms, and so had everybody else, but a photograph was just one flake. One flake could be a coincidence. She wanted to know whether it was a pattern, something true about snow everywhere, or only true sometimes, the way some dogs have spots and some don't.

Outside, the air smelled clean, nothing like the toxic whiff of the furniture polish her mom had been using in the hallway last night. Maya held the dark mitten out flat and stood very still. Flakes landed on the wool and held their shapes for a second before melting. She bent close. Six arms. She brushed the mitten clean and waited for another. Six arms again, this one lacy like a feather. A third flake, small and plain, like a tiny plate. Six. She started keeping count on her fingers, one finger for every flake that agreed.

Alexe arrived with his sled over his shoulder, saw her standing statue-still with her arm out, and asked what on earth she was doing. "Counting arms," Maya said. "Every flake so far has six. Watch." He crouched beside her, breath steaming, and caught some flakes on his own dark sleeve. A big one landed, and they leaned over it together. One, two, three, four, five, six. "Weird," Alexe said. "They're all different shapes, but the number never changes." Maya nodded. That was the strange part. Big, small, lacy, plain, spiky, the arms added up the same way every single time.

After a while the snowfall reached a plateau, steady and even, no longer gusting, and the two of them went inside for hot chocolate. Maya pinned the black mitten on the corkboard by the kitchen window, beside the drawing she had made for Mr. Katz, a snowflake with six arms shaded carefully in blue pencil. At school she was supposed to make a poster where each drawing had to symbolize one thing about winter, and now she knew exactly what hers would be. She dipped the pencil in her cocoa by accident, wiped it on her sleeve, and drew another one, counting the arms out loud as she went.

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: In many cities, each councillor is elected to represent one area of the city, often called a ward.
story:
Penelope had the petition drafted, printed, and stuck to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a rooster, because the bylaw she wanted to change was about roosters. Well, about chickens in general. The city allowed only two hens per yard, and her three hens were, technically, one illegal hen over the limit. "We need ten signatures before Monday," she told Louis-Thomas, who had come over supposedly to help but was currently lying on the kitchen floor with Gumdrop the excessive hen standing on his chest.

"I'll get signatures," Louis-Thomas said. "I'm going to be the signature guy. My signature will be the best one." He held up a hand to examine it, and Gumdrop pecked at his ring, which was a bottle cap, which he had earned from somewhere and would not explain.

First, though, came the email, and that was where Penelope got stuck. She wrote to the councillor whose name she'd seen on a sign near school, explaining everything in her most persuasive font. The reply came back within an hour, and it was polite and useless. "The wrong one," Penelope groaned. She read it again, and a line near the bottom snagged her attention. Each of us represents one area of the city, it said. Contact the councillor for your ward. "Ward," she said out loud, tasting the word. "There's a word for it. It's called a ward."

"So you emailed the wrong neighbourhood's guy," Louis-Thomas said from the floor. "That's like yelling at the thermostat because your house is cold. Doesn't matter how loud, wrong machine." He sat up, dislodging Gumdrop, who expressed her opinion loudly.

Penelope tested it. She typed her street address into the city website, and a map bloomed on the screen, her block sitting inside a purple blob like a grape in jam. Ward 4. Councillor's name, email, even a phone number. "It's not one big pool of councillors," she said, mostly to herself, watching the neighbouring wards press in against hers like puzzle pieces. "It's like the city got cut into slices, and each slice gets its own person." She started a fresh email, and this time she knew exactly where it was going. Somewhere outside, Ms. Santos, who wanted fresh eggs more than anyone on the street, was banging a shovel against a frozen flowerbed in a way that suggested she would sign anything Penelope put in front of her.

The reply from Ward 4 arrived at dinner. Penelope read it with one eye while eating with the other, mostly. The councillor wanted to meet, at city hall, next Thursday. "You can conquer city hall," her dad said, passing her the salt.

"Thursday," Penelope said. She looked down at Louis-Thomas, who had not moved from the floor and was now letting Gumdrop eat crumbs off his sleeve. "Wear your bottle cap ring. We're going to be professional."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Jewish law waives the Yom Kippur fast when health is in danger, and in that case a person is actually required to eat or drink.
story:
Dominic had been hungry since breakfast, and the hunger was the whole point. It was Yom Kippur at his grandpa's apartment, and for the first year his mom had said he was old enough to fast until sundown, the way the whole family did. He sat at the kitchen table watching his cousin Collin, who was ten like him and was slicing an apple into careful pieces.

"You're eating?" Dominic asked, and then he worried it might humiliate Collin, saying it out loud like that, in front of Grandpa. On Yom Kippur, of all days.

Collin didn't look embarrassed. "Rabbi Fine talked to me and my dad on Tuesday," he said. "I have to eat. Insulin and stuff." He pushed the plate across the table. "Jewish law waives the fast when health is in danger. In that case a person is actually required to eat or drink. That's what the rabbi said, almost word for word."

Dominic turned this over. He had assumed fasting meant being hungry, the way a lens meant light bending through glass, one thing causing another, no exceptions. But here was Collin, doing the opposite of fasting and doing it because of the day, not in spite of it. He tried an experiment on himself: he imagined skipping his own fast anyway, just a glass of water, to see whether it would feel like cheating or like nothing much. It felt like cheating. Which meant, he decided, that the rules weren't really about food at all, or not only about food. Something was being asked of him that Collin was excused from, and something was being asked of Collin that he was excused from.

Later that afternoon he wrote a message to his friend Trinity, who was always telling him about her Sunday mornings at her church, and he wanted to get the words right before he spoke them. "I messed up last month when I laughed at your grandma's fasting rule," he typed. "I thought it was just going without stuff. It's more like a promise you keep in your body. Collin's keeping his differently today and it counts exactly the same."

Trinity wrote back a whole paragraph about her grandmother, who used to skip the fast and felt terrible about it for years, until somebody told her what Dominic had just figured out.

At sundown Grandpa put the bread on the table and everyone drank water, even Collin, and Dominic drank his slowly, like it was the answer to a question he was still halfway through solving. Collin grinned at him across the table. "Tomorrow," Collin said, "I'll show you how to fold the paper shofar my dad taught me."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: According to the USDA, a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as its door stays closed.
story:
The lights went out right in the middle of Muhammad's favorite show, and he let out a groan loud enough for the whole street to hear. "Not tonight!" He fumbled to the kitchen and opened the fridge, just to check if the fridge light still worked. It didn't. He grabbed a cheese stick and shut the door. Ten minutes later he opened it again. His conscience gave him a small poke, but the crackers were calling his name, and the cold air spilling over his feet felt too good to give up.

His older sister appeared in the doorway holding a candle like she was leading an expedition. "Third time you've opened that fridge. I counted."

"It's my snack," Muhammad said. "I have to see what's in there."

"You can't see anything in there. It's pitch black." She set the candle on the counter. "Ms. Halvorsen told our class about this. According to the USDA, the fridge keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as the door stays closed. So stop peeking."

Muhammad did the math fast, because math in a crisis felt important. "Four hours? It's only seven o'clock. The ice cream could survive till eleven!" He slammed a sticky note on the fridge door and wrote, in giant letters, DO NOT OPEN UNTIL 11:00. Then, because rules made him feel official, he retired the old cheese stick to his pocket, where it would bother no one.

He texted Mannat right away, because news this big had to travel. The phone glowed in the candlelight like a tiny second moon. His message read: "POWER CUT. FRIDGE ON A SECRET MISSION. IT HAS FOUR HOURS OF COLD LEFT, BUT ONLY IF NOBODY OPENS THE DOOR. THIS IS THE MOST PRESTIGIOUS JOB IN THE HOUSE. I AM GUARDING IT." Mannat wrote back: "my fridge is unguarded. sending my brother over." Muhammad laughed so hard the candle flame wobbled.

Then the lights flickered, buzzed, and blazed back on. The TV roared to life, the fridge hummed its victory hum, and Muhammad yanked his sticky note off the door and held it up like a championship banner. "Four hours!" he shouted. "We didn't even need one!" He flung the freezer open just to feel the cold air on his face, and his sister snatched the handle and pulled it shut again.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A pet microchip is about the size of a grain of rice and holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details.
story:
Joseph rode home from the animal shelter with the carrier strapped to the rack behind his bike seat, and inside it, a gray kitten named Pepper mewing at every bump. He had pumped the tires that morning, working the pump handle like a piston until the tires were rock hard, because today could not be spoiled by a flat. Now the shelter paperwork flapped in his back pocket, and every pedal stroke felt like a victory lap.

Halfway down Maple Street, Aliya came running out of her driveway so fast she nearly collided with his front wheel. "Wait, stop! Is that my Whiskers? He got out three days ago and he's gray too." She crouched at the carrier, and her face fell and lifted at the same time, unsure.

Joseph's heart did a strange double beat. What if the shelter had made a mistake? Then he remembered the worker at the front desk waving a small handheld wand over Pepper's shoulders, and a number popping up on its screen. "It's called a microchip," Aliya said, peering closer. "It's about the size of a grain of rice." Joseph had presumed the scan was just shelter paperwork, the same as signing his name twice, but now he understood it was something better. The chip held an ID number, and a scanner reading it could find the owner's contact details.

"Then we can test it," Joseph said, already turning his bike around. "They scanned Pepper and got my mom's phone number, because we just registered. If Whiskers has one, they'd get your number, not mine. So Pepper isn't yours." Aliya gave him a look that would have been venomous if looks could sting, but she was already grabbing her own bike.

Back at the shelter, the worker waved the wand over Pepper one more time, and the screen showed Joseph's mother's number, right where it belonged. Aliya sagged against the counter, half disappointed and half relieved, and asked if she could put up a poster for Whiskers by the door. The worker handed her tape.

"Race you home," Joseph said, and Pepper mewed through the carrier grate as if she approved.
